chunks.content: By age 18, 7% of all children in the Global North have lost a parent or sibling (Burns et al., ). One in ten bereaved children is at risk of Prolonged Grief Disorder (PGD) (Melhem et al., ). Similar rates have been found in bereaved adults (Lundorff et al., ). Unlike typical bereavement responses, which are characterized by stable, healthy functioning after a loss or by a brief period of distress in the first weeks following bereavement (Nielsen et al., ; Nijborg, Westerhof, et al., ; Pociunaite et al., ), people with PGD experience prolonged and intense bereavement-related distress that impairs functioning (Killikelly et al., ). PGD has only recently been recognized as a mental disorder. It was included in the text-revised fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5-TR; American Psychiatric Association, ) and in the eleventh edition of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11; World Health Organization, ). It is characterized by persistent separation distress (e.g. preoccupation with thoughts or memories of the deceased) alongside cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms (e.g. intense loneliness as a result of the death). PGD symptoms are distinct from posttraumatic stress and depression symptoms in children and adults (Boelen et al., ; Geronazzo-Alman et al., ; Heeke et al., , ; Lenferink et al., ). PGD can be diagnosed six months after a loss in children (and 12 months after a loss in adults). Without treatment, PGD severity tends to remain stable and may continue to hinder children’s functioning (Melhem et al., ). PGD intensity in children and adolescents is commonly assessed using self-report measures. Several instruments are available to assess PGD severity based on prior conceptualizations of disturbed grief, such as the Traumatic Grief Inventory for Children (Dyregrov et al., ), Inventory of Prolonged Grief for Children and for Adolescents (Spuij et al., ), Inventory for Complicated Grief-Revised for Children (Melhem et al., ), and the Persistent Complex Bereavement Disorder Checklist (Kaplow et al., ). These existing instruments do not capture all DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD criteria, such as an inability to experience positive mood, feelings of blame, denial, and emotional numbness. Moreover, they include items assessing grief reactions that are not part of the DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 PGD criteria, such as sleep difficulties, hearing the voice of the deceased, or seeing the deceased. Recently, the Traumatic Grief Inventory-Kids-Clinician-Administered (TGI-K-CA) was developed, with input from bereaved children, adolescents, and experts. The TGI-K-CA assesses interview-based PGD intensity and probable caseness in children (aged 8–18) based on the most recent PGD criteria as defined in DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 (Van Dijk et al., ). An initial psychometric evaluation of the 16-item TGI-K-CA in 90 Dutch bereaved children (8–18) shows strong internal consistency for items assessing DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD, although some items showed poor factor loadings. The latter pertains to items assessing the symptoms about marked sense of disbelief (in DSM-5-TR), denial (in ICD-11), avoidance (in DSM-5-TR), blame, guilt, and anger (all in ICD-11). These items also showed floor effects, which may indicate that these symptoms are either rare in this age group or not optimally captured by the current item formulations, suggesting a need for further refinement of age-tailored wording. Furthermore, strong convergent validity, but weak temporal stability, was found, pointing to the possibility that grief in children fluctuates considerably over time. Optimal cut-off scores for detecting probable PGD caseness for DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD items (when summed separately) were ≥29 and ≥33, respectively. These cut-off scores were ≥45 and ≥53 when summing all 16 items (van Dijk et al., ). To date, instruments assessing PGD intensity in children have relied primarily on self-report. However, parents or caretakers may observe behavioural and emotional changes, such as anger, that children themselves may not recognize (Kassam-Adams et al., ). Moreover, some children may also be unable or unwilling to share their feelings due to factors like stigma (Breen et al., ). In addition, direct assessment of children and adolescents is not always feasible or practical. For instance, parents often initiate help-seeking on behalf of their children, and children are generally a hard-to-reach population in research. Parental or caregiver reports, therefore, provide a valuable alternative and can play a crucial role in screening for PGD in children and adolescents (Stover & Keeshin, ). To the best of our knowledge, only one instrument to date has been developed to assess caregiver-reported ICD-11 PGD intensity in children, namely the caregiver-report version of the International Grief Questionnaire (IGQ-CG) (Redican et al., ). In a sample of 639 Ukrainian caregivers, support was found for a correlated two-factor latent structure of the ICD-11 PGD items. Separation distress (factor 1) and cognitive, behavioural, and emotional items (factor 2) loaded on two separate, but strongly related, factors. for PGD in children and adolescents (Stover & Keeshin, ). To the best of our knowledge, only one instrument to date has been developed to assess caregiver-reported ICD-11 PGD intensity in children, namely the caregiver-report version of the International Grief Questionnaire (IGQ-CG) (Redican et al., ). In a sample of 639 Ukrainian caregivers, support was found for a correlated two-factor latent structure of the ICD-11 PGD items. Separation distress (factor 1) and cognitive, behavioural, and emotional items (factor 2) loaded on two separate, but strongly related, factors. The items showed acceptable internal consistency and convergent validity (as indicated by expected associations with other mental health outcomes, time since loss, and PGD intensity in caretakers). This 5-item measure assesses seven out of 12 ICD-11 PGD symptoms, i.e. items assessing the symptoms ‘denial’, ‘blame’, ‘feeling one has lost a part of one’s self’, ‘an inability to experience positive mood’, and ‘difficulty in engaging with social or other activities’ are lacking. Moreover, some of the items assess two symptoms simultaneously (e.g. ‘they feel guilty or angry about their loss’). To capture the full spectrum of PGD symptom intensity in children through caregiver-reports, a caregiver-report version of the TGI-K-CA was developed. This instrument intends to assess caregiver-ratings of PGD symptom intensity in children per DSM-5-TR and ICD-11. This enables comparisons of diagnostic performances of these criteria-sets. In this initial validation study, we evaluated the psychometric properties of the Traumatic Grief Inventory-Kids-Caregiver-report (TGI-K-CR). As found in prior validation research on caregiver-report measures for PGD intensity (Redican et al., ), we expected to find support for a two-factor structure and strong internal consistency. In terms of known-groups validity, we expected that, similar to research on trauma symptoms in children (Egberts et al., ; Kassam-Adams et al., ), that caregivers who identify as women (vs. man) and those who reported higher PGD intensity themselves would report higher PGD intensity in their child. Moreover, based on literature reviews (Alvis et al., ; Falala et al., ), we anticipated higher caregiver-ratings of PGD intensity in children, when the child was identified as a girl (vs. boy), the loss was more recent, due to a potential traumatic circumstance (i.e. accident, homicide, suicide), and when the child had lost a nuclear family member (parent or sibling vs. other loss). Lastly, percentages of probable caseness for DSM-5-TR and ICD PGD were calculated, and provisional cut-offs for both criteria-sets were determined, enabling the distinction of probable PGD cases from non-cases. 1. Methods 1.1. Participants and procedures Data were collected via a public website ( www.rouwbehandeling.nl ) providing information about grief, prolonged grief, and professional grief support. One of the facilities of this website is to offer a free online self-test for adults to monitor PGD intensity in children (this is called the ‘Grief monitor for children’). Before completing this self-test background- and loss-related characteristics are completed. Then, caregivers are asked to complete the TGI-K-CR. After completing this self-test, an outcome of the test is provided based on their responses. Optionally, caregivers can also complete a self-test to monitor their own grief reactions using the TGI-SR+, as well as their child, using a self-report version of the TGI-K-CA. The self-test users were asked at the end if their responses could be used for scientific purposes. A local ethics committee approved this study (University of Twente, ID: 231153). Data-collection took place between March 2024 and June 2025. In total, 218 caregivers completed the grief monitor for children and provided consent for their data to be used for research purposes. Seven of those reported the loss of a pet or separation of parent, and 16 reported that the child was aged >18 years. After exclusion of these responses, the final sample consisted of 196 caregivers who completed the TGI-K-CR. Among them, 66 caregivers also reported on their own PGD symptoms. Only 32 children reported on their own symptoms. The latter were, therefore, not included in this study. 1.2. Measures 1.2.1. Prolonged grief intensity in the child reported by the caregiver Caregiver-ratings of PGD intensity in children were assessed with the TGI-K-CR. This is a 16-item self-report survey for caregivers to rate PGD intensity in their child in the past month. This measure is similar to the TGI-K-CA, which is an interview developed for clinicians to screen for PGD intensity in children (aged 8–18). The only difference is that we ask for caregiver – instead of child-ratings (e.g. ‘Did you miss ____very much?’ is now rephrased as ‘Did your child miss ____very much?’). Answers were provided on 5-point Likert scales, 1 = never, 2 = rarely, 3 = sometime, 4 = often, 5 = always. For DSM-5-TR PGD, items 1–11 represent each one symptom, except that items 6 and 7 both represent the symptom ‘Intense emotional pain (e.g. anger, bitterness, sorrow) related to the death’. The only difference is that we ask for caregiver – instead of child-ratings (e.g. ‘Did you miss ____very much?’ is now rephrased as ‘Did your child miss ____very much?’). Answers were provided on 5-point Likert scales, 1 = never, 2 = rarely, 3 = sometime, 4 = often, 5 = always. For DSM-5-TR PGD, items 1–11 represent each one symptom, except that items 6 and 7 both represent the symptom ‘Intense emotional pain (e.g. anger, bitterness, sorrow) related to the death’. The highest score on item 6 (‘Was your child very sad because … has died?’) and 7 (‘Was your child very angry because … has died?’) was used as an indicator for that specific symptom. Total DSM-5-TR PGD scores range from 10 to 50. For ICD-11 PGD, items 1–4, 6–9, 12–15 were used to represent each symptom. Total ICD-11 PGD scores range from 12 to 60. See Supplementary Table 1 for item-mapping of TGI-K-CR items on DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD symptoms. 1.2.2. Prolonged grief intensity in the caregiver reported by the caregiver PGD intensity in caregivers was assessed using the 22-item Traumatic Grief Inventory-Self Report Plus (TGI-SR+), which has been validated in various bereaved adult samples across the globe (Chaebin et al., ; Cherblanc et al., ; Kokou-Kpolou et al., ; Lenferink, Eisma, et al., ; Lenferink, Johnsen, et al., ; Lenferink, van Dijk, et al., ; Lenzo et al., ; Tang et al., ; Treml et al., ). This self-report measure assesses DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD symptom intensity using 5-point Likert scales. An example item is: ‘In the past month, I had trouble accepting the loss’. Sumscores of 71 or higher are indicative of probable PGD caseness. The original Dutch version has good psychometric properties. This measure has been translated into 20 languages (see: https://osf.io/rqn5k/files/osfstorage ). Cronbach’s alpha in the current study was .90. 1.2.3. Background- and loss-related characteristics The following background characteristics were assessed by caregivers: gender and age of caregiver and child, cause of death (illness, accident, suicide, homicide, other), caregiver and child relationship to the deceased, and time since loss. 1.3. Statistical analyses 1.3.1. Factor structure The factor structure for DSM-5-TR PGD and ICD-11 PGD items was examined using confirmatory factor analyses (CFAs) in Mplus version 8.6 (Muthén & Muthén, ). The item scores were normally distributed as indicated by kurtosis values below 10 and skewness values below 3. Therefore, we used maximum likelihood estimation. We compared the model fit of a two-factor model (factor one including items assessing separation distress symptoms and factor two including items assessing cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms) with a one-factor model. Model fit evaluation was based on: (1) Comparative Fit and Tucker Lewis Indices (CFI and TLI) values >0.90 representing acceptable fit and >0.95 excellent fit, (2) Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) values <0.10 representing acceptable and <0.05 excellent fit. Lower Akaike, Bayesian, and Sample-Size adjusted Bayesian information criteria (AIC, BIC, and SS-BIC) were preferred when comparing the one- and two-factor models for DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 separately (Kline, ). Chi-Square tests were used to test if the fit of the two-factor model significantly improved compared with the one-factor model. The TGI-K-CR items had no missing data. 1.3.2. Internal consistency McDonald’s Omgea (ω) values were computed for evaluating internal consistency of DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD items separately (while excluding the functional impairment item). We considered ω > 0.70 acceptable (Hayes & Coutts, ). 1.3.3. Known-groups validity Pearson’s correlation analyses were used to examine associations between DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD intensity on the one hand and PGD intensity of caregiver and time since loss on the other hand. Independent t -tests were used to examine associations between DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD intensity and gender of caregiver, gender of child, cause of death (natural cause vs. accident, homicide, suicide, other loss) and death of a nuclear family member as reported for the child by the caregiver ((step)parent or (step)sibling vs. other loss). 1.3.4. Rates of cases versus non-cases using diagnostic scoring rules Using the diagnostic scoring rule for DSM-5-TR PGD items, at least one separation distress, at least three out of eight cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms, and the functional impairment item (item 16) should be endorsed for probable caseness. For ICD-11, at least one separation distress, at least one of 10 cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms, and the functional impairment item (item 16) should be endorsed for probable caseness. Often, a more conservative diagnostic scoring rule for probable caseness of ICD-11 PGD is used, in which at least five of 10 cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms should be endorsed (Lenferink, van Dijk, et al., ; Tang et al., ; Treml et al., ). For ICD-11, at least one separation distress, at least one of 10 cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms, and the functional impairment item (item 16) should be endorsed for probable caseness. Often, a more conservative diagnostic scoring rule for probable caseness of ICD-11 PGD is used, in which at least five of 10 cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms should be endorsed (Lenferink, van Dijk, et al., ; Tang et al., ; Treml et al., ). A score of at least 4 (‘often’) was considered a symptom endorsed. 1.3.5. Optimal cut-off to detect probable PGD caseness Optimal cut-off scores were determined to detect children who met versus did not meet probable DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 PGD caseness using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analyses. First, we determined an optimal cut-off score for the summed DSM-5-TR PGD item scores (range 10–50; excluding the functional impairment item), the summed ICD-11 PGD item scores (range 12–60; excluding the functional impairment item), followed by the summed TGI-K-CR total score (range 16–80). Again, the liberal and conservative diagnostic scoring rules for ICD-11 PGD were used. Based on the sensitivity and specificity rates, a Younden’s index was calculated. A Younden’s index < .70 was interpreted as poor accuracy, between .70 and .80 as fair, and between .80 and .90 as good, and >90 as excellent in detecting PGD caseness (Ferraris, ). 2. Results 2.1. Characteristics of the caregiver, child, and the loss Four out of five caregivers (82%) identified as women. About half of the children (47%) were identified as girls. The average age of the caregivers was 44 (range 16–85), and the average age of the children was 11 (range 8–18). In 77% of the cases, the loss was due to an illness. In 44% of the cases, the child lost their parent. The losses happened on average 21 months earlier (range 1–344). See for details. Mean scores for PGD intensity in children as reported by caregivers were 27.91 (SD = 7.27) for DSM-5-TR (when summing 10 items), 31.57 (SD = 8.21) for ICD-11 PGD intensity (when summing 12 items), and 41.62 (SD = 11.09) when summing all 16 items. These mean scores were 26.80 (SD = 7.53), 30.11 (SD = 8.40), and 40.05 (SD = 11.42), respectively, when including only those whose loss occurred at least 6 months earlier ( N = 110). See Supplementary Table 1 for mean item-scores and floor effects (i.e. caregivers reporting the lowest possible item score). 2.2. Factor structure of DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD items in children rated by caregivers shows the fit indices of the one- and two-factor CFA models for DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 items. For DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, the two-factor model showed a significantly better fit than the one-factor model based on lower AIC and BIC values and significant χ2 difference tests (DSM-5-TR: Δχ 2 = 31.15 (1), p < .001; ICD-11: Δχ 2 = 26.24, p < .001). However, the CFI, TLI, and RMSEA values were not acceptable for the two-factor model for DSM-5-TR and ICD-11. Modification indices indicated that error-terms of some item-pairs were strongly correlated for DSM-5-TR (i.e. item-pairs C3-C6 and B1-C3). These correlations likely stem from content overlap between items C3 and C6 as both reflect avoidance of internal and external reminders of the loss. Regarding item-pair B1-C3, these items reflect the approach-avoidance paradox in grief, where people both seek closeness to the deceased and attempt to avoid the pain associated with the loss (Eisma & Lenferink, ). Similar results were found for ICD-11, where item-pair C5-C10 reflects similar content in terms of wording referring to ‘other people’. Item-pair C2-C9 shows similarities as both items contain emotionally charged words related to the loss. When correlating the error terms for two item-pairs, the fit indices were acceptable for the two-factor models for DSM-5-TR and ICD-11. These two factors were significantly ( p < .001) correlated (DSM-5-TR: r = .758; ICD-11: r = .789). displays the factor loadings of the two-factor models. For DSM-5-TR, three items had poor factor loadings (i.e. <.600), namely the items assessing the symptoms avoidance, marked sense of disbelief about the death, and emotional numbness. For ICD-11, the following five items had poor factor loadings: disbelief about the death, anger, emotional numbness, guilt, and blame. 2.3. For ICD-11 PGD items, the internal consistency was ω = .87 for all caregivers and ω = .88 for those whose loved one died at least 6 months earlier ( N = 110). 2.4. Internal consistency For DSM-5-TR PGD items, the internal consistency was ω = .85 for all caregivers and ω = .88 for those ( N = 110) whose loved one died at least 6 months earlier. For ICD-11 PGD items, the internal consistency was ω = .87 for all caregivers and ω = .88 for those whose loved one died at least 6 months earlier ( N = 110). 2.4. Known-groups validity DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD intensity in children, as rated by caregivers, were positively related to caregivers’ own PGD intensity ( r = .34, p = .006 for DSM-5-TR PGD; r = .32, p = .009 for ICD-11 PGD) and negatively to time since loss ( r = −.19, p = .008 for DSM-5-TR PGD; r = −.21, p = .004 for ICD-11 PGD). T-tests showed that PGD intensity in children did not differ based on caregiver’s gender ( t (192) = −1.40, p = .164 for DSM-5-TR PGD; t (192) = −1.34, p = .181 for ICD-11 PGD) or child’s gender ( t (193) = −0.41, p = .682 for DSM-5-TR PGD; t (193) = −0.45, p = .651 for ICD-11 PGD). No significant differences were found in PGD intensity in children in terms of cause of death ( t (194) = −0.59, p = .558 for DSM-5-TR PGD; t (194) = −0.79, p = .430 for ICD-11 PGD) and child’s relationship to the deceased ( t (194) = −0.66, p = .510 for DSM-5-TR PGD; t (194) = −1.09, p = .279 for ICD-11 PGD). 2.5. Rates of cases versus non-cases using diagnostic scoring rules Sixty-two children (32%) met probable DSM-5-TR PGD criteria. One hundred nine (56%) met probable ICD-11 PGD caseness when using the liberal scoring rule for ICD-11 PGD, and 15 children (8%) met probable ICD-11 PGD caseness using the conservative scoring rule. When including children only whose loss occurred at least 6 months ago ( N = 110), these rates were 26%, 46%, and 7%, respectively. 2.6. Optimal cut-off score for probable PGD caseness When summing the 10 DSM-5-TR PGD items only, we found that a score of ≥29 optimally distinguished probable DSM-5-TR PGD cases from non-cases (AUC = 0 .946; 95% CI: 0.918–0.974). Using this cut-off score resulted in correctly identifying 95% of probable DSM-5-TR PGD cases and 21% incorrectly identifying these cases ( J = 0.74). When summing the 12 ICD-11 PGD items only, we found that a score of ≥31 optimally distinguished probable ICD-11 PGD cases from non-cases (AUC = 0 .888; 95% CI: 0.843–0.932) using the liberal diagnostic scoring rule. This cut-off resulted in correctly identifying 81% of probable ICD-11 PGD cases and 20% incorrectly identifying these cases ( J = 0.61). When using the conservative scoring rule, we found that a score of ≥41 optimally distinguished probable ICD-11 PGD cases from non-cases (AUC = 0 .983; 95% CI: 0.962–1.000). This cut-off resulted in correctly identifying 93% of probable ICD-11 PGD cases and 8% incorrectly identifying these cases ( J = 0.86). When summing all 16 items, we found that a score of ≥46 optimally distinguished probable DSM-5-TR cases from non-cases (AUC = 0 .888; 95% CI: 0.843–0.932). This cut-off resulted in correctly identifying 84% of probable DSM-5-TR PGD cases and 12% incorrectly identifying these cases ( J = 0.72). For ICD-11 cases using the liberal diagnostic scoring rule, we found that a score of ≥39 optimally distinguished probable ICD-11 cases from non-cases (AUC = 0 .868; 95% CI: 0.819–0.918). This cut-off resulted in correctly identifying 84% of probable ICD-11 PGD cases and 25% incorrectly identifying these cases ( J = 0.58). For ICD-11 cases using the conservative diagnostic scoring rule, we found that a score of ≥52 optimally distinguished probable ICD-11 cases from non-cases (AUC = 0 .979; 95% CI: 0.959–0.100). This cut-off resulted in correctly identifying 100% of probable ICD-11 PGD cases and 11% incorrectly identifying these cases ( J = 0.89). 3. Discussion This is a first examination of the psychometric properties of a survey assessing DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD intensity in children as reported by caregivers. This instrument, called the TGI-K-CR, is based on the TGI-K-CA. The latter is a clinician-administered interview to assess PGD intensity in children, which was co-developed using cognitive interviews with bereaved children and experts (Van Dijk et al., ). While in the TGI-K-CA, items are completed by the child, we now rephrased the items so that caregivers rate the PGD intensity of their child. Caregiver-ratings may overcome challenging situations where it may not be possible or practical to assess PGD in children and adolescents directly. as reported by caregivers. This instrument, called the TGI-K-CR, is based on the TGI-K-CA. The latter is a clinician-administered interview to assess PGD intensity in children, which was co-developed using cognitive interviews with bereaved children and experts (Van Dijk et al., ). While in the TGI-K-CA, items are completed by the child, we now rephrased the items so that caregivers rate the PGD intensity of their child. Caregiver-ratings may overcome challenging situations where it may not be possible or practical to assess PGD in children and adolescents directly. We first examined the factor structure of the DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD items separately. As expected, we found support for two distinct but related factors. This means that the two symptom clusters, (1) separation distress and (2) cognitive, behavioural, and emotional symptoms, as proposed by DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, each represent a unique aspect of PGD as an underlying construct, while still being correlated with one another. This aligns with prior research in caregiver-ratings of PGD in children as well as with self-rated PGD intensity in adults (O’Connor et al., ; Redican et al., ; Tang et al., ). While we found support for strong internal consistency, some of the factor loadings were poor. More specifically, we found poor factor loadings for the items assessing the symptoms ‘marked sense of disbelief/denial’, ‘avoidance’, and ‘emotional numbness’ in DSM-5-TR. In addition, the items assessing ‘marked sense of disbelief/denial’, ‘emotional numbness’, ‘anger’, ‘guilt’, and ‘blame’ had poor factor loadings for ICD-11. Relatively poor factor loadings were found for these items in self-reported PGD levels in children (Spuij et al., ; van Dijk et al., ) as well as in adults (Lenferink, Eisma, et al., ). It has been suggested that these poor factors may have partially been attributable to floor effects of these specific items (van Dijk et al., ). Indeed, we found that for some items (i.e. ‘marked sense of disbelief/denial’, ‘guilt’, and ‘blame’) caregivers more often responded that their child ‘never’ experienced these symptoms compared to other symptoms, indicating that these symptoms are rarely observed or reported by children without and with probable PGD. These poor factor loadings may also partially reflect developmental differences in how PGD symptoms manifest in children (Alvis et al., ). For instance, concepts such as disbelief, guilt, and blame may be cognitively or emotionally less developed in children compared to adults. As a result, children may be less likely to experience these responses following loss and/or these reactions may be less observable by caregivers, leading to relatively poorer factor loadings of these items in caregiver reports of PGD in children compared to adults' self-rated PGD levels (Lenferink, Eisma, et al., ). Similarly, avoidance and emotional numbness may be expressed in more behavioural or indirect ways in children (vs. in adults). For instance, children may experience reduced emotional vocabulary to express themselves emotionally, or use distraction in activities (e.g. gaming) as an avoidance strategy, or try to stay strong for their caregivers out of protection (Breen et al., ). These developmental manifestations are not fully captured by the current wording of the items. Hence, future research could examine whether the operationalization of these symptoms requires further developmentally sensitive adaptations to better reflect how such grief reactions are expressed across age groups (Van Dijk et al., ). However, other items with poor factor loadings did not show these floor effects (and some items with similar floor effects showed strong factor loadings), indicating that these poor factor loadings are only partially explained by limited variability in response patterns. Given that across children, adolescents, and adults, using different PGD measures, relatively poorer factor loadings are consistently found for ‘avoidance’, ‘marked sense of disbelief/denial’, ‘guilt’, ‘anger’, and ‘blame’ (Ergun et al., ; Killikelly et al., ; Lenferink, Eisma, et al., ; O’Connor et al., ; Spuij et al., ; van Dijk et al., ), this may signal at least three issues that are related to the conceptualization and/or measurement of PGD in general, rather than developmental manifestations unique to PGD in children. First, some symptoms, such as guilt, blame, or anger, may be particularly relevant in people bereaved by potentially traumatic losses, such as guilt in suicide-bereaved people (Hofmann et al., ; Linde et al., ), while blame and anger are common in people bereaved by traffic accidents or homicides (Boelen et al., ; Lenferink, Nickerson, et al., ; Nijborg, Kunst, et al., ; van Denderen et al., ). These items may therefore have less discriminant ability to distinguish probable cases from non-cases after non-traumatic causes of death. Second, some symptoms may be difficult to assess using ratings from caregiver- or self-report, such as avoidance (Gamez et al., ). This can be explained by the approach-avoidance paradox of PGD (Eisma & Lenferink, ) that holds that approach behaviours (such as yearning for the deceased)

al., ), while blame and anger are common in people bereaved by traffic accidents or homicides (Boelen et al., ; Lenferink, Nickerson, et al., ; Nijborg, Kunst, et al., ; van Denderen et al., ). These items may therefore have less discriminant ability to distinguish probable cases from non-cases after non-traumatic causes of death. Second, some symptoms may be difficult to assess using ratings from caregiver- or self-report, such as avoidance (Gamez et al., ). This can be explained by the approach-avoidance paradox of PGD (Eisma & Lenferink, ) that holds that approach behaviours (such as yearning for the deceased) may act as avoiding the reality of the loss. A more elaborate clinical diagnostic interview may tackle this issue (O’Connor et al., ). Third, some symptoms rarely occur together because they are mutually exclusive; for example, feeling emotionally numb may not often occur alongside intense sadness or anger when assessed retrospectively in the past month. Assessing multiple symptoms using one item, as was done earlier by Redican et al. ( ; e.g. ‘They feel sad or emotionally numb’), may solve this issue in future research. An even more promising approach would be to use real-time assessments rather than retrospective assessments to capture the dynamic nature of grief (Lenferink, Terbrack, et al., ; Marcolini et al., ). Although empirical evidence is still lacking, it has been suggested that grief reactions may fluctuate even more in children than in adults (Child Bereavement UK, ; Russell et al., ), which could also account for the weak temporal stability of the TGI-K-CA observed in prior research (van Dijk et al., ). Next, we found partial support for known-groups validity. As expected, we found that caregiver ratings of PGD in children were positively, significantly, and moderately related to caregivers’ own PGD intensity. This has also been shown in adult parent-child dyads (Lenferink & O’Connor, ). Our findings now suggest that grief transmission effects may also apply to caregiver-child dyads, including minor children. We also found a weak, but significant, association between time since loss and caregiver-ratings of PGD intensity in children, which aligns with prior research (Alvis et al., ). Unexpectedly, we did not find that caregiver-ratings of PGD intensity in children varied in terms of the gender of the caregiver or child, nor in terms of cause of death and relationship to the deceased. However, other studies also found mixed results regarding some of these variables and PGD intensity in children (Alvis et al., ). Also, our limited sample size, in particular, the relatively small number of male caregivers and children bereaved by potentially traumatic causes, likely resulted in limited statistical power to detect possible group differences. When determining optimal cut-off scores to detect probable PGD caseness, we found that a cut-off score of ≥29 can fairly detect probable DSM-5-TR PGD caseness. The same cut-off score was found for the child self-report version of this instrument (van Dijk et al., ). For ICD-11, a cut-off of ≥31 seems optimal when using the liberal diagnostic scoring rule that included the presence of at least one accessory symptom, but this resulted in too many false positives. This false-positive rate was reduced when using the conservative scoring rule (of at least five accessory symptoms), which showed that a cut-off score of ≥41 optimally distinguished probable ICD-11 PGD cases from non-cases with good accuracy. The latter was also found for the self-report version of this instrument for adults (Lenferink, Eisma, et al., ). When summing all 16 items, we found that a score of ≥46 and ≥52 optimally distinguished probable cases from non-cases for DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 PGD, respectively, with sufficient accuracy. These cut-offs were similar (i.e. ≥45 and ≥53, respectively) to the ones found when using self-report ratings in children using the child-version of this instrument (van Dijk et al., ). At least four limitations should be considered when reading this work. First, in total, 196 caregivers participated, but among them, only 66 completed the TGI-SR + to rate their own PGD intensity. This resulted in limited statistical power for our correlation analyses. Moreover, unfortunately, only 32 children reported on their own PGD intensity. On the one hand, this points to the relevance of relying on caregiver-ratings for PGD intensity in children, because self-reported data on PGD intensity in children is difficult to obtain. On the other hand, due to a lack of self-reported child data, we were unable to explore agreement between caregiver and child ratings of PGD intensity in children. Second, for determining probable PGD caseness and cut-off scores, a diagnostic interview is ideally used. Future research should use both surveys and interviews to compare their diagnostic performance. Third, our survey was limited in length, and our design was cross-sectional. Therefore, we were not able to test some important indices of validity, such as convergent

for PGD intensity in children, because self-reported data on PGD intensity in children is difficult to obtain. On the other hand, due to a lack of self-reported child data, we were unable to explore agreement between caregiver and child ratings of PGD intensity in children. Second, for determining probable PGD caseness and cut-off scores, a diagnostic interview is ideally used. Future research should use both surveys and interviews to compare their diagnostic performance. Third, our survey was limited in length, and our design was cross-sectional. Therefore, we were not able to test some important indices of validity, such as convergent validity, test–retest reliability, predictive validity, and longitudinal measurement invariance. Fourth, our sample consisted of a convenience sample of caregivers who expressed their interest in grief treatment by completing the TGI-K-CR on a website named ‘grief treatment’. This self-selection bias likely limits the generalizability of our findings, for instance, to caregivers who are not interested in grief treatment. To finalize, this initial validation of the TGI-K-CR is a first step to enable empirical research into PGD intensity, as defined by DSM-5-TR and ICD-11, in children based on caregiver-ratings. Clinicians may use this instrument as a time-efficient screening tool for early identification of PGD. Summing all 16 items, using the cut-off score of ≥46 for DSM-5-TR PGD and ≥52 for ICD-11 PGD is recommended when assessment relies on caregiver-ratings, which are very similar to those used for children’s self-report ratings (i.e. ≥45 and ≥53, respectively). However, a thorough clinical assessment remains essential for diagnosing PGD. The relatively poor performance of several items indicates that developmental differences in the manifestation of grief may not be sufficiently captured by current screening tools relying on the current classification systems. These developmental aspects should receive greater attention during clinical intake to minimize the risk of misclassification. Researchers may use this instrument to enhance our knowledge on the prevalence, predictors, and treatment of PGD in children. This may facilitate more research into PGD intensity in children, which is urgently needed given that grief research in children is sparse, while 7% of all children face the death of a parent or sibling before the age of 18 (Burns et al., ). We cautiously conclude that the TGI-K-CR appears to be a promising screening tool for PGD in children (aged 8–18) using caregiver-reports. Supplementary Material Supplemental Material

What is known? • Both the number of studies and the scope on pediatric palliative care improved from 2004 to 2018. However, the research focuses and trends have not been investigated yet. What is new? • Integration palliative care into pediatrics, pediatric palliative care interventions, methods to improve quality of life, and pain management in pediatric palliative care were the focuses from 2004 to 2018. • Communication skills between professionals and parents, the methods of resolving ethical issues, family support and evidence-based guidelines are potential hotspots in the future. 1 Introduction According to the estimate of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately 2000 children had life-limiting diseases (LLDs) in the year 2017 in the USA, and the number had been increasing year by year [ ]. Connor et al. estimated that more than 21 million children needed pediatric palliative care (PPC) [ ]. When firstly put forward in the paper titled Dying children need help too by Chapman and Goodall [ ], PPC aroused great attention. In 1998, PPC was officially defined as “the active total care of the child’s body, mind, and spirit, and also involved in giving support to the family and it began when illness was diagnosed, and continued regardless of whether or not a child received treatment directed at the disease” [ ]. Since 2003, PPC has been recognized as a pediatric sub-specialty by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) [ ], and more and more researchers have noticed that children with LLDs need more attention. In fact, PPC is far more different from the palliative care for adults [ ], especially in care skills such as communication skills with children’s parents and dealing with bereavement care [ ]. For example, types of diseases, treatments, and various needs in different age groups. Moreover, 13.6% of the children are undiagnosed, which increases the psychological burden of the parents [ ]. Although it is extremely suffering from losing a child, some parents gradually accept palliative care (PC) so that their children can go through the last period of life without over-treatment and unbearable suffering. To better meet the increasing needs on PPC, the number of relevant research papers is increasing, focusing on different topics, such as suffering relief of the children [ ], improving the quality of life of the whole family [ , ], and the therapy of neoplasms [ ]. Besides, the scope of studies on PPC has also been greatly extended from the children， parents [ ], and children’s siblings [ ] to the whole family [ ]. Bibliometrics was defined as “the study and measurement of the publication patterns of all forms of written communication and their authors” [ ], which took quantitative characteristic as research objects to analyze structural distribution, quantitative relation, and management of literature using math and statistic [ ]. Bibliometrics has been widely applied in biomedicine, psychiatry, military nursing [ ], nursing management [ ] and genomic nursing [ ], but not in PPC as far as we could search in literature. Although there have been a large number of PPC related studies, the research focuses and trends remain unexplored. Therefore, it is meaningful to sort out the focuses, describe the dynamic trends, and predict the future research directions on PPC using bibliometric analysis methods. In this study, 2004 was the starting year because PPC became an independent subspecialty in 2000 in the United States [ ] and subsequently it was recognized as a specialty by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and Royal College of Nursing in 2003 [ ]. Formal recognition of a subspecialty or specialty by official organizations sets standards on which healthcare staff can rely [ ]. And 2018 was the ending year as the last search was run in July 2019. Fifteen years between 2004 and 2018 were equally divided into three periods: 2004–2008, 2009–2013, and 2014–2018, in reference to a systematic scoping review on palliative care [ ]. This study aimed to 1) identify the research focuses in the past 15 years, 2) describe the changing trends of the three periods, and 3) predict the research trends in the future. 2 Methods 2.1 Design Quantitative bibliometric analyses on PPC studies from 2004 to 2018 were carried out to figure out the research focuses and predict future directions. 2.2 Data collection (((“Child"[MeSH]) OR “Pediatrics"[MeSH])) AND (“Terminal Care"[MeSH] OR “Palliative Care"[MeSH] OR “Hospice Care"[MeSH]) for the literature search in PubMed database. The results were collected based on three periods, namely from January 1, 2004 to December 31, 2008 (2004–2008), from January 1, 2009 to December 31, 2013 (2009–2013), and from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2018 (2014–2018). Since “pediatric” is spelled as “pediatric” in British English, the use of “pediatrics” as the MeSH term ensured complete research results.

on PPC studies from 2004 to 2018 were carried out to figure out the research focuses and predict future directions. 2.2 Data collection (((“Child"[MeSH]) OR “Pediatrics"[MeSH])) AND (“Terminal Care"[MeSH] OR “Palliative Care"[MeSH] OR “Hospice Care"[MeSH]) for the literature search in PubMed database. The results were collected based on three periods, namely from January 1, 2004 to December 31, 2008 (2004–2008), from January 1, 2009 to December 31, 2013 (2009–2013), and from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2018 (2014–2018). Since “pediatric” is spelled as “pediatric” in British English, the use of “pediatrics” as the MeSH term ensured complete research results. The language of the articles was limited to only English and the text availability was limited to full text. There was no restriction of article type as well as both “child” and “pediatric” were used so that we could enlarge the sample size to conduct the analyses more comprehensively. The primary results showed 571 literature published between 2004 and 2008, 748 between 2009 and 2013, and 939 between 2014 and 2018. Subsequently, we checked the titles, abstracts, and full-texts (if necessary, namely the full-texts of studies needed to be read when we couldn’t exclude or include the studies according to the titles and abstracts) to screen out those irrelevant papers among the primary results ( n = 2,258). We double-checked the included records based on the relevance of PPC. Finally, we included 1,132 articles ( ) and exported the data with the “XML” format. The ethics approval for this study was not required due to reusing pre-existing literature in this study. 2.3 Data extraction and the formation of matrix Co-word analysis can identify the relations of professional terms in relevant articles, based on the occurrence frequency of these terms, and demonstrate the theme structure changes [ ]. In this study, the frequency of MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings was calculated by Bibliographic Item Co-Occurrence Matrix Builder (BICOMB), and the high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings were sorted into clusters by Graphical Cluster Toolkit (gCLUTO). BICOMB is a text mining system based on the co-occurrence of bibliographic items in literature databases, which was developed by Cui et al. in 2008 [ ]. BICOMB can be used to sort out the MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings, publication years, countries, journals, authors and generate a co-occurrence matrix of the MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings. H-index was chosen to identify the high-frequency major MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings, which was first introduced by Hirsch to evaluate the research output of individuals [ ]. H-index was calculated according to a previously reported method [ ]. Firstly, the high-frequency entries were arranged according to the descending order of frequency, and the entries whose word frequency was greater than or equal to their serial number ( h ) were found out from the list of high-frequency entries, and the frequencies of subsequent terms were less than h . Thus, h was taken as the threshold for intercepting high-frequency terms, and the high-frequency MeSH terms-source article matrix was generated according to the intercepted high-frequency terms. Therefore, we respectively exported the high-frequency MeSH terms-source article matrix and co-occurrence matrix of the three periods. 2.4 Biclustering analysis Biclustering analysis was proposed by Hartigan to sort heterogeneous data into a homogeneous block by constructing clusters of variables or cases [ ]. Based on the high-frequency MeSH terms-source article matrix, gCLUTO 1.0 software ( http://glaros.dtc.umn.edu/gkhome/cluto/gcluto ) was utilized to conduct the biclustering analysis and create matrix visualization and mountain map. In this study, repeated bisection was selected as the biclustering method, cosine was selected as the similarity function, and I 2 was selected as the criterion function. Following the principles that external similarity (ESim) should be as small as possible while internal similarity (ISim) should be large, we constantly adjusted the number of clusters to obtain the optimal results. In the mountain map, the height of the peak is directly proportional to the ISim and the volume is proportional to the number of MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings each mountain contains. The distance between clusters stands for the similarity. Different colors of red, yellow, green, light blue, and dark blue are shown in the mountain map, but only the color of the peaks is informative, which represents the internal standard deviation (ISdev), such as red for small ISdev and blue for large ISdev. Red peaks indicate that the similarity of the articles within a cluster is high and the major topics of each cluster are consistent, while blue peaks mean that high variation among the contents. Through the biclustering analysis, the clusters of the three periods were generated. The semantic relations such as causation and influence relation among the high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings within a cluster were used in combination with the representative articles of each cluster to conclude the theme of corresponding high-frequency MeSH terms. 2.5 Strategic diagram analysis Strategic diagram analysis was

The semantic relations such as causation and influence relation among the high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings within a cluster were used in combination with the representative articles of each cluster to conclude the theme of corresponding high-frequency MeSH terms. 2.5 Strategic diagram analysis Strategic diagram analysis was firstly introduced in 1988 by Law et al. [ ], which was described as a 2D coordinate system to show the structure of a field. In other words, it aimed to visually depict the position in the coordinate system of clusters and compared the trends of clusters in 3 periods by calculating the internal association within one cluster and external influences among the clusters. In detail, the x-axis stands for centrality, which represents the influences of clusters on each other by measuring the strength of links among clusters; the y-axis stands for density, representing the development conditions of a cluster by measuring the strength of internal association of MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings within this cluster. According to the co-occurrence matrix, each cluster’s centrality and density were calculated, and the 2D strategic diagram was subsequently delineated. The specific calculation method was illustrated by Callon et al. [ ]. The meaning of a strategic diagram is as follows: x-axis (namely density) means internal closeness within the cluster, indicating the ability to sustain and develop itself, whereas y-axis (namely centrality) means external closeness with other clusters, indicating the degree to interact with other clusters. Clusters in quadrant 1 with high centrality and density mean themes of these clusters are the focuses. Quadrant 2 involves clusters with high density but weak centrality, which means they are specialized and less integrated with other disciplines. Clusters with both low centrality and density in quadrant 3 are emerging or outdated and these clusters are less interconnected not only within the cluster but also among other clusters. Clusters with strong centrality but weak density in quadrant 4 mean that although they are closely correlated with other clusters, internal development within the cluster is still immature. 3 Results 3.1 Distribution of the research output The 1,132 papers included in this study between 2004 and 2018 were divided into three groups based on the publication time. In general, the number of studies was steadily rising, with 293 published between 2004 and 2008, 396 between 2009 and 2013, and 443 between 2014 and 2018. The numbers of studies refined by the items of country, journal, and author are shown in . Most of the articles were published based on research departments in the United States, England, and Germany. Journal of Palliative Medicine has maintained the top highly produced journal since 2004. The authors with the largest numbers of published papers during the three periods were Jones BL, Knapp C, and Downing J, respectively ( ). 3.2 High-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings and the results of biclustering analysis High-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings during the three periods were ranked to conclude the corresponding themes since they represent the research focuses. The matrix visualizations show that there were 42 high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings between 2004 and 2018, and the number was 12 between 2004 and 2008, 13 between 2009 and 2013, and 17 between 2014 and 2018, which were listed on the right side of , , B, respectively. The left hierarchical trees indicate the relationship among the high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings, and the top ones represent the relationship among the term-resources articles. Besides, these 12 high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings between 2004 and 2008 can be classified into five clusters ( A). Likewise, the 13 high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings between 2009 and 2013, and 17 high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings between 2014 and 2018 can be classified into five clusters ( A) and 6 clusters ( A), respectively. As shown in the mountain map ( , , A), there are red peaks of cluster 2 (establishment of a PPC team) of the first period, cluster 2 (professional-family relations) and 3 (interventions on PPC) of the second period, and cluster 2 (pain management in PPC) of the third period. According to the calculated results, the clusters fell in different quadrants, representing the development conditions of them. For the results of the articles published during 2004–2008, cluster 0 (integration palliative care[PC] into pediatrics) is in the first quadrant. Cluster 1 (cancer treatments in pediatric oncology), 2 (establishment of a PPC team), 3 (education methods on PPC), and 4 (parents’ attitude to their child’s death) are in the third quadrant. And the results between 2009 and 2013 show that clusters 1 (methods to improve quality of life in PPC) and 3 (interventions on PPC) are in quadrant 1. Cluster 0 (palliative care in pediatric intensive care units) is located in quadrant 3. Quadrant 4 includes clusters 2 (professional-family relations) and 4 (ethics on PPC and attitude of health personnel in PPC). For the results in the last period, cluster 2 (pain management in PPC) is in quadrant 1. Clusters 0 (attitude of health personnel in PPC) and 4 (communication skills on PPC) are included in the second quadrant. Cluster 1 (family support in PPC) is in quadrant 3. And clusters in quadrant 4 are clusters 3 (end-of-life decision-making in PPC) and 5 (guideline making on PPC). 4 Discussion 4.1 Interpretation of the results More and more researchers, especially health professionals in the pediatric oncology field have been studying PPC, and progress has been made in the past 15 years. In this study, co-word analysis, biclustering analysis, and strategic diagram analysis were combined to identify the research focuses in different periods and reveal the trends in the past 15 years. Although the amount of literature on PPC was increasing, there was a problem that most of the studies were carried out in developed countries instead of being distributed evenly in the world. It can be explained to some extent that there were better economic conditions, policy-making, medical systems, curriculum design, personnel training, and well-established policies in the developed countries at the onset of the studies on PPC [ , ]. Besides, the liberal and sociocultural context is also supposed to be taken into consideration [ ]. We suggest that the developing countries or regions learn the advanced experiences from the developed countries while considering the local situation, to establish their own completed systems. More remarkable and novel findings are expected in a variety of regions to further promote the development of PPC [ , ]. The trends in the changes of the research themes can be explained that the integration of pediatric oncology and PC was the focus and well-developed in the first period. The status quo of palliative care in pediatric oncology, caring for a dying child [ ], and education for physicians [ ] had been reported during 2004–2008. Place of death, cause of death, funding of PPC, and bereavement care were the most mentioned of the literature in this period [ , , ]. The frequent place of death for children with life-limiting conditions was shifted gradually from hospital to community. The percentage of in-hospital death decreased from 83.8% in 2004 to 68.1% in 2014 in England [ ]. It was also reported that the establishment of a PPC team [ ], including professional palliative care teams, psychotherapists, and priests, would facilitate the implementation and development of PPC. Cancer treatments in pediatric oncology, the establishment of a PPC team, education methods on PPC, and parents’ attitude to their child’s death were the emerging topics during 2004–2008. It is plausible that these clusters will move to other quadrants as time goes by because studies on PPC are becoming more and more popular. There were many fresh ideas but immature in this period. Subsequently, quality of life improvement and PPC interventions were focuses in the second period (2009–2013). Most of these interventions were non-pharmaceutical therapies [ , ]. For example, music therapy for children in the terminal stage was an effective way to relieve physical and psychological suffering while improving quality of life. Meanwhile, it helped to enhance family bonding and strengthen family cohesion in tough times. In addition, some undeveloped topics were showing up, such as ethics on PPC, attitudes of health personnel in PPC and professional-family relations during 2009–2013. improvement and PPC interventions were focuses in the second period (2009–2013). Most of these interventions were non-pharmaceutical therapies [ , ]. For example, music therapy for children in the terminal stage was an effective way to relieve physical and psychological suffering while improving quality of life. Meanwhile, it helped to enhance family bonding and strengthen family cohesion in tough times. In addition, some undeveloped topics were showing up, such as ethics on PPC, attitudes of health personnel in PPC and professional-family relations during 2009–2013. As for ethics, healthcare staff often encountered ethical dilemmas in caring for dying children, such as truth-telling, the best ethical decision making, and do-not-resuscitate (DNR) [ , ]. For the family, medical decisions of children generally relied on the parents’ willingness, which was influenced by income, relationship, and education. Children were more willing to be included in informing the medical progress, even in the decision about death [ , ]. Thus, the voice of children also needs to be further explored. It was essential to suit preferred ethical options for individuals, which varied in different sociocultural contexts and political systems. The attitude of professionals directly influenced the clinical practice, patients’ feelings, parents’ choices and development of PPC [ ]. Attitudes of health personnel depended on how they experience in the caring or treating and the knowledge and skills on PPC they got [ ]. Barriers including uncertain prognosis, language barriers, and time constraints frequently or almost always occurred during the caring, which might lead to the staff members’ negative emotions, resulting in changes in their attitude [ ]. PC in pediatric intensive care units became less focused in this period due to comprehensive research in the first period. In the third period, we can find that health personnel’s attitude [ ] moved from quadrant 4 in the second period to quadrant 2, which also was an improvement from immature to mature. Professional-family relations emphasized offering psychological support in the second period, and communication skills were indispensable to maintain and improve the relationship [ , ]. Some high-frequency MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings in the second period, such as parents’ attitude to death [ ] and ethics on PPC [ ] reoccurred in the third period. It is worth noting that the same themes may show up in different periods. It may be because studies on the same themes were first conducted in developed countries or regions and gradually extended to other developing countries or regions. Furthermore, some new topics emerged, such as communication skills [ ] and guideline making on PPC [ , ] during 2014–2018. Based on this, we can reasonably speculate that communication skills, guideline making, or policy setting may become the future research hotspots. Besides, there is only one cluster in the quadrant 1 in the first period, indicating superficial research on PPC; there are two clusters in the quadrant 1 and 4 in the second period; finally, there are clusters in every quadrant in the third period, demonstrating the researching scope was expanding. The three strategic diagrams show that the MeSH subheading (organization and administration of PPC) shows up in every period, suggesting that it takes a long time to build a specialized and collaborative team to work on PPC [ ]. According to our findings, the research trends in the future were concluded as follows. Ethics on PPC was in quadrant 4 in the second period, indicating studies on these themes have been carried out yet still under development. Ethical dilemmas within PPC faced by healthcare staff were mainly conflicting over the right to treatment and withholding, decision-making in the child’s best interests and communication [ ]. Effective approaches discussed by treatment teams, parents, children and bioethics committees to deal with these issues are required in the future. In the third period, communication skills was in quadrant 2, showing that indistinctive progress has been made on these themes. The difficulties and experiences of professionals when delivering end-of-life discussion in PPC have been reported [ , ]. Nevertheless, training programs on communication skills were still inadequate. Family support was in the quadrant 3 in the third period, indicating family-centered approaches compared to patient-centered ones were a newly-developing area. Family support was included in the definition of PPC, and the child and family should be treated as a unit [ ]. Although the whole family was affected by the child’s illness, most studies focused on parents’ needs recently, and the experiences and needs of siblings or even grandparents need to be discovered. Guideline making was in quadrant 4 in the third period, demonstrating that they have advanced to the middle level with a great promise in the future. Guidelines focused on the PPC concepts, principles and models from policymakers’ or societal perspectives in the last two decades, while these theoretical guidelines may not be suitable

definition of PPC, and the child and family should be treated as a unit [ ]. Although the whole family was affected by the child’s illness, most studies focused on parents’ needs recently, and the experiences and needs of siblings or even grandparents need to be discovered. Guideline making was in quadrant 4 in the third period, demonstrating that they have advanced to the middle level with a great promise in the future. Guidelines focused on the PPC concepts, principles and models from policymakers’ or societal perspectives in the last two decades, while these theoretical guidelines may not be suitable to the complex and dynamic medical settings [ ]. In addition, guidelines on bereavement care pathways, multidisciplinary teams and critical assessments are needed [ ]. End-of-life decision-making was also in quadrant 4 in this period. End-of-life decision making should involve parents and other family members, professionals and the child. The attitudes of parents, nurses and physicians on the decision-making process and the factors influencing the final decision have been discussed. However, the child’s own thoughts and preferences on the decision-making need to be explored [ ]. 4.2 Limitations Even though we employed three analysis methods to conduct a comprehensive study as much as possible, there are still some limitations. Literature in Web of Science and PubMed could be analyzed by BICOMB. The MeSH terms/MeSH subheadings were sorted out for literature in PubMed while keywords were sorted out for literature in Web of Science. In addition, the number of included studies in PubMed was more than those in Web of Science. And the final included studies in PubMed contained the studies that met the inclusion criteria in Web of Science. Therefore literature was only chosen in PubMed as MeSH terms are only available in this database. More comprehensive research conditions may be acquired by employing more databases with the implementation of more advanced software in the future. In addition, only the publications of English studies were searched, which may have resulted in missing some points. 5 Conclusion In this study, we analyzed the research focuses in three periods of the past 15 years and compared the number of publications and trends in the changes of research themes, aiming to provide evidence of PPC development for researchers, policymakers, and leaders. The results suggest that PPC is in a developing period, with an increasing number and variety of literature but an uneven research distribution in the world. Because of the uneven global distribution of the studies, other countries or regions can develop their models on PPC according to the local situation based on those in the lead. The conclusions are as follows. 1) Integration PC into pediatrics, interventions on PPC, methods to improve quality of life, and pain management were the focuses from 2004 to 2018. 2) The trends in the changes of the research themes followed the sequence. Integration PC into pediatrics, cancer treatments in pediatric oncology, education methods, and professional team establishment were the major themes during 2004–2008. Then the themes changed into establishing interventions to enhance the life quality of the patients and parents, building professional-family relationships, and investigating the attitude of healthcare staff during 2009–2013 and subsequently turned into communication skills, end-of-life decision making, and guideline making on PPC during 2014–2018. 3) Ethical dilemmas within PPC, training programs on communication skills, family support for children who have life-limiting diseases, and evidence-based guidelines from different countries are potential hotspots in the future. documents.title: EAPC Position Paper on Euthanasia and Physician-Assisted Suicide

chunks.content: Introduction Recently, a marked evolution in how death is socially conceptualised and negotiated has been observed [ ]. In clinical practice, despite remarkable technological advances and uprising expectations for successful outcomes across even the most invasive interventions [ ], over half of critically ill patients die before hospital discharge, with nearly 20% of these deaths occurring in the intensive care unit (ICU) [ ]. Hence, ICU stay remains a therapeutic trial without guarantees [ ]. Aggressive interventions often do not meaningfully improve outcomes, increasing patient suffering while placing emotional and financial strain on families [ , ]. These end-of-life (EOL) situations raise complex ethical dilemmas [ ]. In response, practices such as withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment have been developed [ ], grounded in bioethical principles and widely integrated into clinical protocols [ , , ]. In tandem, advance directives (ADs) and decision-making models grounded on patient autonomy are also increasingly incorporated into EOL care [ , - ]. Respect for individual autonomy also remains a key argument in favor of euthanasia and physician-assisted dying (PAD) - both of which have been linked with landmark legal cases, wide media coverage and a growing regulatory and legislative activity in some jurisdictions [ , ]. Euthanasia, PAD, and EOL decisions remain among the most ethically and socially complex areas in medicine [ , ]. Their framing and public perception vary widely worldwide, shaped by diverse cultural and systemic factors [ , - ]. Key concepts surrounding euthanasia, physician-assisted dying and EOL decision-making remain inconsistently defined and distinguished [ , - ], whereas public attitudes toward EOL issues are underexplored [ , ]. Literature remains fragmented, often addressing euthanasia, PAD, and EOL issues separately, with little or vague conceptual integration [ ]. At the same time, existing debates mainly reflect North American or Western European settings and focus mostly on clinicians’ or relatives’ perspectives [ , , ], limiting their relevance in culturally and systemically distinct contexts. Across diverse national settings, euthanasia and PAD remain illegal [ ], while the framework for ADs, EOL practices, and decision-making remains both underdeveloped and ambiguously defined [ - ]. Existing instruments focus on clinicians or family perspectives and do not fully address the public or all relevant concepts cohesively, even across different sociocultural and legal contexts [ - ]. Ηence, a pressing need is identified to investigate relevant public attitudes across the social spectrum in a clear, distinct and conceptually cohesive way, particularly in settings with varying regulatory frameworks and cultural backgrounds [ , , - ]. To address this gap, the Physician-assisted dying, Euthanasia, Advance Directives, and Care at the End-of-life Questionnaire (PEACE-Q) was developed. It is a novel self-report instrument designed with adaptability as a core feature to ensure international applicability across diverse sociocultural and legal contexts. It captures societal perspectives by addressing each thematic section autonomously, while at the same time providing a holistic existential orientation toward end-of-life issues and death, systematically integrating the ethical, legal, religious and practical dimensions that shape relevant attitudes. Its design allows adaptation to various regulatory frameworks and cultural settings, making it applicable in countries with differing approaches to euthanasia, PAD, and EOL care. The present study pursues the following objectives: (a) to describe the development of the PEACE-Q through a systematic multistage process; (b) to evaluate its psychometric properties; and (c) to assess its validity and reliability as an instrument for measuring public attitudes toward euthanasia, PAD, ADs, and EOL practices. Initial validation was conducted within a large Greek population-based sample - a setting characterized by strong religious traditions, an underdeveloped regulatory framework and ongoing public debate on EOL issues. Beyond its research utility, findings derived from the PEACE-Q's application may inform clinical communication, ethical debate, and policymaking, and support its deployment as an international tool across diverse cultural and regulatory contexts. Materials and methods Instrument development The PEACE-Q was developed through a multistage process to ensure conceptual clarity, content validity, and psychometric robustness. Before commencing data collection, the PEACE-Q was developed following international recommendations for the design and adaptation of self-report measures [ ]. The development process was structured to create a tool adaptable to various regulatory and cultural settings, while initial validation was conducted in Greece. It was constructed through a four-stage process: (a) item generation from literature review and comparative analysis of existing tools, (b) drafting of items designed for cross-cultural applicability, (c) review by an expert panel of intensivists, lawyers and psychologists, and (d) pilot cognitive debriefing with laypersons (N = 50) to ensure clarity and cultural relevance within the Greek context. The final version incorporated adjustments based on pilot feedback and was proofread for linguistic accuracy and consistency. The final design allows for adaptation to different legal frameworks - including jurisdictions where euthanasia and PAD are legal, illegal, or undergoing legislative change

Greece. It was constructed through a four-stage process: (a) item generation from literature review and comparative analysis of existing tools, (b) drafting of items designed for cross-cultural applicability, (c) review by an expert panel of intensivists, lawyers and psychologists, and (d) pilot cognitive debriefing with laypersons (N = 50) to ensure clarity and cultural relevance within the Greek context. The final version incorporated adjustments based on pilot feedback and was proofread for linguistic accuracy and consistency. The final design allows for adaptation to different legal frameworks - including jurisdictions where euthanasia and PAD are legal, illegal, or undergoing legislative change - while maintaining its core structure and psychometric properties. It evaluates public attitudes by addressing personal, ethical, legal and religious dimensions of the investigated concepts, aiming to explore how individuals understand, relate and respond to them within the framework of their personal values, faith, and autonomy regardless of their sociocultural background. The full English version of the instrument is available in the Appendix Section. Ethical considerations The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the University of Ioannina (Approval No. 48956) in accordance with institutional guidelines and the principles of the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments. Participation was strictly voluntary, anonymous, and based on informed consent. Research context and participants Data collection was implemented through a nationwide cross-sectional survey, disseminated across all regions of Greece. Questionnaires were distributed and collected consecutively between January and June 2025. The study population consisted of adult (≥18 years) Greek citizens, residing in Greece, regardless of sociodemographic characteristics. Only one response per individual was accepted. The questionnaires were distributed nationwide via a secure online platform (Google Forms), accessible without login or personal identifiers to ensure anonymity. A snowball sampling strategy was applied to ensure broad participation from all geographic regions of the country. The estimated completion time was 15-20 minutes. To enable test-retest reliability analysis, participants were asked to generate a personal identification code (derived from non-identifying family initials and date of birth patterns), allowing to match responses without compromising anonymity. Upon completion, responses were exported into Excel format, then converted into JAMOVI, SPSS, and R datasets for analysis. All data were stored on encrypted, password-protected devices accessible only to the research team. Measurements The introductory sociodemographic module includes items about age, sex, residence, educational status and employment. Additional items capture prior ICU exposure, professional background in healthcare, close contacts with health professionals and religiosity. All items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale and multiple-choice formats. Section A includes 19 Likert-type items addressing conceptual distinctions between euthanasia and PAD, ethical and legal acceptability, need for legal regulation, willingness to request euthanasia/PAD in severe illness and the perceived influence of religion. This section engages with autonomy and self-determination, as well as ethical dilemmas surrounding the occurrence of death. Section B comprised 10 Likert-type items exploring participants’ perspectives on ADs and healthcare proxies, focusing on willingness to prepare, trust in close persons as proxies, readiness to assume the role of proxy for others and the perceived need for legal regulation. This section captures both attitudes toward advance care planning and the broader ethical-legal considerations that shape decision-making at the end of life. Section C contains 21 Likert-type items examining perceptions of treatment withdrawal, withholding of life-sustaining interventions, and Do-Not-Resuscitate orders. It assesses personal and ethical perspectives, perceived moral equivalence of different EOL practices, roles of clinicians and families in decision-making, willingness to endorse the implementation of EOL practices and palliative care, as well as attitudes toward legal regulation and religious influence. Data analysis An integrated analytic strategy was adopted to ensure both structural and item-level evaluation of the questionnaire. First, an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted using principal component analysis (PCA) with Varimax rotation to identify the underlying factor structure. Factors were retained based on the Kaiser criterion (eigenvalues > 1) and items were assigned to the factor on which they showed the highest loading [ , ]. This method was selected because our primary aim at this stage was exploratory - mapping the structure of attitudes rather than modelling latent constructs - and because the hypothesised sections were considered conceptually distinct. The use of PCA with orthogonal rotation facilitated a parsimonious and interpretable factor structure, supported by the large sample size. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was not selected because the dimensional structure of the adapted questionnaires was not yet fully established. This choice is consistent with recommendations that EFA be used in the early stages of psychometric evaluation [ , ]. Second, Item Response Theory (IRT) was applied using the Graded Response Model (GRM), estimated separately for each subscale identified in the EFA [ , ].
